it may be.
אִיּוֹב pr. n. Job, an Arab of Uz or
Ausitis, distinguished for wealth and
also for piety and virtue, but tried of God
with the heaviest calamities. Besides
the book of Job, he is also mentioned in
Ez. 14, 14. 20. Sept, Ἰώβ, Arab. أَيُّوب.
The name signifies pr. one persecuted,
from r. אָיַב, as יִלּוֹד one born, from יָלַד;
and refers to the calamities by which
he was afflicted.—Others render it: serio
resipiscens, i. q. Arab. أَوَّابٌ, from r. אוּב,
آبَ, to return, to convert, comp. Cor.
Sur. 38. 40–44; but see against this,
Thesaur. Ling. Heb. p. 81. col. 1.
אִיזֶבֶל f. (pr. non-cohabited, i. e. ἄλο-
χος Plat. p. 249. B, Lat. intacta, chaste,
comp. Agnes; an appropriate female
name, and not to be estimated from the
character and conduct of Ahab’s queen;)
Jezebel, Isabella, pr. n. of a notorious
woman, the daughter of Ethbaal king
of Tyre, and wife of Ahab king of Israel,
infamous for her idolatry and cruel per-
secution of the prophets. 1 K. 16, 31.
אֵי־זֶה where? Job 38, 19. 24. Com-
pounded from the interrog. part. אֵי, אַי
q. v. no. 2, and זֶה here.
אֵיךְ how? apoc. from אֵיכָה, Gen. 26,
9. Without interrogation, Ruth 3, 18.
2 K. 17, 28.—Often as an exclamation
of pain or grief, how! Ps. 73, 19. Is. 14,
אֵיכָה from אֵי no. 2, and כָּה i. q. כֹּה
so, here.
1. how? in what way? Deut. 1, 12.
Without interrogation, Deut. 12, 30.
2. where? Cant. 1, 7.
3. Often as an exclamation of pain or
grief, how! like אֵיךְ, Is. 1, 21. Lam. 1, 1.
אֵיכֹה (id.) where, not interrogative,
once 2 K. 6, 13, where Keri has אֵיכוֹ id.
אֵיכָכָה (Milêl) how? Cant. 5, 3. Esth.
8, 6. From אֵי and כָּכָה i. q. כָּה, כֹּה, so.
אֱיָל see r. אוּל.
אַיִל m. 1. a ram, so called from his
twisted horns, q. d. rolled up; see r. אוּל.
Gen. 15, 9. Plur. אֵילִים Ex. 25, 5, and
אֵלִים Job 42, 8.—Hence intens. אַיָּל q. v.
2. A term of architecture, referring,
as it would seem, to a projection in a la-
teral wall, serving as a post or column,
i. e. a pilaster; either from r. אוּל no. 3,
or like Lat. aries, capreolus, Germ. Bock,
used for a buttress. 1 K. 6, 31. Ez. 41,
38; comp. v. 26. 31. 34. 37. The ancient
versions render it sometimes posts, some-
times columns. See Boettcher’s Proben
alttestamtl. Schrifterkl. p. 302.
אַיָּל m. a stag, hart, male deer, Deut.
2, 9. 17. Always masc. but in Ps. 42, 2
joined with a fem. in the manner of
comm. gend. thus denoting a hind, which
elsewhere has the specific name אַיָּלָה,
אַיֶּלֶת. Chald. and Syr. id. Arab. أَيَّل
wild goat, mountain-goat, chamois. Eth.
ኀየል, by which orthography the affinity
of the roots אוּל and חוּל is distinctly con-
firmed.—As to the etymology, אַיָּל is a
sort of intensive of אַיִל, therefore pr. a
large ram or buck, and אַיָּלָה a large she-
goat or the like. Indeed the Hebrews
would seem to have called all the va-
rious species of deer and antelopes, which
in part are furnished with twisted horns
like the ram, by the general name of
large rams or wild rams; just as the
Germans call the same animals Berg-
ziegen, wilde Ziegen, and the Latins
capreæ, from their general resemblance
to a goat, capra. Sept. every where
ἔλαφος.
אֱיָל m. strength, might, once Ps. 88, 5.
R. אוּל no. 2.
אַיִל m. (r. אוּל) plur. אֵילִים, pr. strong,
stout, mighty.
1. Plur. the mighty, the powerful, the
nobles of a state, city, Ex. 15, 15. Ez. 17,
2. a strong, stout, mighty tree, like δρῦς,
spec. the oak, terebinth, and sometimes
also the palm, i. q. אֵלָה, אַלּוֹן, which is
more usual. Sing. once Gen. 14, 6 in
the pr. n. אֵיל פָּארָן, Sept. τερέβινθος τῆς
Φαράν. Plur. אֵילִים, אֵלִים Is. 1, 29. 57,

line_status.note: A maqqef is printed between אֵי and זֶה (the top bar runs continuously from the yod into the zayin); Reading A omits it. Vowels (tsere under alef, segol under zayin) and the rest of the line agree with both readings.
The first word after "i. q." has a qamets under the dageshed kaph (כָּה), not a holam; only the second word carries the holam (כֹּה). Reading A wrongly repeats כֹּה twice.
Aleph carries hataf-segol (two vertical dots + stroke) and yod carries a T-shaped qamets; the patach/hireq form אַיִל is the headword of line 2 ("a ram"), not line 1.

The last Hebrew word shows a dagesh dot in the yod and a qamets (T-shaped) beneath it, not a hireq: אַיָּל (the intensive form "stag"), as in Reading A; Reading B's אַיִל would merely repeat the headword.

No accent is printed on the lamed — the only stroke above it is the lamed's own ascender; the word is plain אֵילִים (tsere, yod, hiriq, yod, mem), so Reading B's ֫ is spurious. Rest of the line identical in both.

The Arabic alif carries its hamza (with fatha) ABOVE the letter, not below, and no kasra is printed under it; shadda+fatha on the yā'. Reading A puts hamza below with kasra, B drops the hamza — both wrong.

The first Ethiopic glyph is printed with a top bar, a slanted stroke and a barred vertical stem — the shape of ኀ (ḫa), not the open U-shape of ሃ (hā). The rest (የል and the English) is identical in both readings.
Both vavs carry a visible shureq dot in the print (אוּל, חוּל); Reading A omits them.
The vowel under yod is printed as a qamets (bar with stem) with a dagesh in the yod, giving אַיָּל (stag), not hireq אַיִל (ram) as in Reading B.
